name: PT Dharma Satya Nusantara Tbk

frontmatter.title: Dharma Satya Nusantara: an estate priced for a weaker palm price than the deck
frontmatter.summary: DSNG trades at 4.1x forward operating EBITDA and 7.3x forward earnings while the nine-month operating run-rate sits just under the forecast. The deck's palm price path and a balance sheet with net debt at a fraction of EBITDA support a twelve-month value of Rp2,713, an expected total return of 108.5% against the Rp1,325 price of which 104.8% is price appreciation. Rating BUY.
thesis: The nine-month actual already earns the year: the printed nine-month line of 2,950 IDR bn carries IDR144.4bn of associate profit and an IDR41.4bn biological-asset gain that our operating EBITDA excludes, and stripped of both it annualises a few per cent below the full-year base case of 3,926.0, the gap being the fourth-quarter volume the volume input already carries.
The market pays 4.1x for an estate whose cash cost per tonne is set by the audited accounts rather than by a cycle trough, and whose net debt is small against annual EBITDA.
The deck's palm price path to US$1,240/t rests on the GAPKI forecast of a 2,200 kt fall in Indonesian output, and the reverse DCF says the share price discounts US$1,044/t.

The bear case, which now carries a stronger rupiah and a wider domestic discount as well as a weaker palm price, values the shares at Rp917, below the current price; the base and bull cases carry the asymmetry.
The main risk is policy and weather rather than the balance sheet: the export levy, the biodiesel mandate and El Nino move the domestic price more than any company decision.

catalysts.event: Monthly export duty and levy reset, and the December reference price
Audited accounts for the year to December and the dividend proposal
Annual general meeting and dividend approval

blocks.text: We initiate on Dharma Satya Nusantara with a BUY rating and a twelve-month value of Rp2,713 per share, an expected total return of 108.5% from the Rp1,325 price, of which 104.8% is target-price appreciation and the balance the next-twelve-month dividend. The company is a mid-sized Indonesian oil-palm estate with a wood-products business and a small renewable-energy arm, and the equity is priced as though the palm price has already peaked. At the current price the market capitalisation is IDR14,044.8bn, and enterprise value — market capitalisation plus our forecast net debt for the current year and the minorities — is 4.1x our forward FY2026E operating EBITDA of IDR3,926.0bn, against the 6.6x that the peer and history cross-check supports [S3, S4]. The multiple and the EBITDA are on the same forward year and the same operating definition, which section three sets out in full with the reconciliation to the audited line; on the spot net debt at the end of September the same equity capitalises the same earnings at a slightly higher multiple, and after deducting the associate stake at book it is lower again, which section four sets out [S2, F44].

The reason the multiple is low is visible in the accounts. Nine-month revenue of 9,110 IDR bn was only slightly ahead of the prior year, and the printed nine-month EBITDA of 2,950 IDR bn was flat as well. That line is not our operating measure — it carries the associate's IDR144.4bn and an IDR41.4bn biological-asset gain — but the operating figure is flat too, because El Nino cut fresh fruit bunch production to 1,500 kt while the realised price rose only modestly [S2, S5]. The market reads that combination as the end of the palm cycle. We read it as a volume problem in one region, with a price deck that still points higher and a cost base already reset by the audited accounts [S3, S4].

The balance sheet is the second leg of the case. Net debt at the end of September was small against annual EBITDA, the bond repaid during the last financial year removed the largest single maturity, and finance costs fell as a result [S2, S3]. The company also owns a stake in an associated estate that we carry at book value in the bridge, so the equity value does not depend on a refinancing or an asset sale [S2, F44].

The third leg is the price path. The house deck has CPO at US$1,135/t for the current year, US$1,240/t next year and US$1,150/t in the long run, and GAPKI expects Indonesian output to fall by 2,200 kt in 2027 as the full El Nino effect lands [S8, F37]. Our reverse DCF says the current price discounts a CPO price of US$1,044/t, or 84.2% of the deck's next-year level, so the market is not paying for that supply response [S0, S3].

What would change our mind is a second year of falling volumes without a price response, or a policy change that widens the domestic discount permanently. The first is partly in the base case, which holds volume flat through the GAPKI trough year; the second is not. The bear case, which applies the shocks shown in the scenario table, values the shares at Rp917, below the current price, so the rating rests on the base and bull cases rather than on a downside that protects capital [S3, S6].

DSNG is an integrated oil-palm producer. At the end of the last financial year it managed a planted area of 111,900 ha, of which the nucleus estates are the company's own and the plasma estates are smallholder blocks developed and supervised by the company [S4, F38]. The nucleus area is supported by a set of mills across Kalimantan with a combined processing capacity reported in the annual report, and the certification coverage is broad: every mill is ISPO certified, most are RSPO certified, and all are Halal certified [S4]. The estate is concentrated in East, Central and West Kalimantan, with a large contiguous block in East Kalimantan, which is the operational advantage that a scattered estate cannot replicate [S4].

The product set is broader than crude palm oil. The company sells CPO, palm kernel and palm kernel oil, and it also runs a wood-products business making engineered flooring and panels from two plants in Central Java, plus a renewable-energy business that exports palm kernel shells and wood pellets to Japan [S4, S7]. The palm segment contributed 88.0% of consolidated revenue of 9,110 IDR bn in the first nine months of the current year, with wood products and renewables making up the balance [S7, S2, F54, F31]. The palm segment is therefore the valuation, and the other two segments are optionality that we carry at a modest margin rather than as separate businesses [S3].

Operationally, the last full year was a good one. CPO production reached 631 kt and sales were 629 kt, with fresh fruit bunch production of 2,189 kt and an extraction rate of 23.3% [S4, F23, F1, F25, F26]. The extraction rate fell slightly on the prior year, which the company attributes to the change in fruit composition as the dry weather took hold, and the palm kernel and palm kernel oil volumes grew faster than CPO [S4, F27, F28]. The company also published a production target for the last financial year of 651 kt, which the realisation of 631 kt missed, and projects 637 kt for the current year on its own budget; the nine-month outturn of 451 kt makes even that projection look optimistic [S4, S5, F46, F60, F23, F34].

The strategy is deliberately unglamorous. Management is replanting the older blocks, completing the plasma programme, deleveraging the balance sheet and adding small downstream projects such as a bio-compressed natural gas plant that uses mill effluent [S4, S7]. There is no large acquisition in the plan and no new planting frontier, so the capital allocation question is simply whether the dividend and the replanting budget can both be funded from operating cash flow, which at the last actual they could [S3, F50].

The group structure matters for governance. The company controls its mills and estates through operating subsidiaries, holds an indirect stake in an associated estate in East Kalimantan, and reports a small non-controlling interest [S2, S3, F44]. The controlling shareholders are the families behind the Triputra and Oetomo groups, and the president director is a member of the Oetomo family, so the company is a family-controlled mid-cap rather than a widely held corporate [S4, F55, F56].

Indonesia is the largest producer of palm oil in the world, and the industry is dominated by a handful of very large groups alongside a long tail of mid-sized estates. The economics of an estate are set by the age profile of the palms, the extraction rate, the distance to a mill and the quality of the logistics chain, because the fruit must be processed within a day of harvest. Companies with young estates and integrated mills earn a structural cost advantage that shows up in the cash cost per tonne, and companies with old estates and third-party fruit face a permanent margin penalty. The wood and biomass businesses are small by comparison and are valued on their own cash flows rather than as part of the palm cycle.

The palm price is the single largest driver of the company's earnings, and the house deck has it rising from US$1,007/t in the last actual year to US$1,135/t this year and US$1,240/t next, before fading to US$1,150/t in the long run [S0]. The shape matters more than the level: the deck expects the current supply tightness to peak next year and then ease as new plantings in the wider industry come into production. Our model takes that path as given and translates it into a rupiah price through the realisation ratio and the exchange rate, which is where the company-specific judgement sits [S3, S4].

The supply side is genuinely tight. GAPKI expects Indonesian palm output to fall by 2,200 kt in 2027 as the full effect of the long dry spell is felt, and the association's chairman has said the reduction accounts for the complete El Nino impact rather than a partial one [S8, F37]. The company's own experience is consistent with that: fresh fruit bunch production fell to 1,500 kt in the first nine months, with the third quarter alone down on the second, and CPO output fell to 451 kt over the same period [S5, S7, F35, F34]. A supply decline of that size in the world's largest producer is the reason the deck does not have the price falling back to the last cycle's average [S8].

The policy setting is more complicated, and the November change is not the one-way positive it first looks. The Ministry of Trade sets a reference price each month and derives an export duty and a levy from it; for November the reference price is US$979/t and the combined duty and levy is US$246/t, down a fifth on October [S6, F48, F36]. But the same release shows the reference price falling at the same time, so the net export parity — the reference price less the levy — was essentially unchanged on October: exporters keep a larger share of a lower price, not a larger price [S6]. For a domestic seller such as DSNG — the geographic segment note shows the whole palm line sold into the local market with no export sales [S2, F61] — the relevant variable is the domestic price relative to the world benchmark, which the levy affects only through that net parity; the November package therefore does not narrow the discount in itself. The same report notes that the rupiah was Rp18,140/USD, close to its weakest on record, which raises the rupiah value of every dollar-denominated tonne [S6, F47].

The biodiesel mandate is the other policy pillar. The government confirmed in early November that it will keep the B50 blend, and GAPKI data show palm oil use for biodiesel at 1,350 kt in August while exports rose and stocks fell [S6, F49]. A mandate that absorbs a large and growing share of domestic production supports the domestic price and competes with exports for the same tonnes, which is why the levy and the mandate are best read together rather than separately [S6].

Competitive positioning is a question of cost and certification rather than of market share. DSNG is a small producer against the national total, so it is a price taker, but its cash cost per tonne is set by its own estate and mill efficiency, and its certification coverage is high across the nucleus estates and the mills [S4]. That matters for sales into Europe and Japan, where the wood-pellet and palm-kernel-shell businesses already sell, and it matters for access to sustainability-linked finance, which the company has used [S4, S7].

The moat is therefore narrow but real. The estate is contiguous, the mills are close to the fruit, the extraction rate is above the industry average, and the certification stack is complete enough to sell into premium markets [S4, F26]. What the company does not have is pricing power, because the product is a commodity and the domestic price is set by a formula linked to the export reference price [S6]. That is why we value it on a through-cycle price rather than on a multiple of the current spot, and why the cost side of the model is built from the audited accounts rather than from an industry average [S3].

The palm oil industry is cyclical and politically exposed. Prices are set in a global market where the main substitutes are soya oil, sunflower oil and rapeseed oil, and the spread between them moves with weather, energy prices and trade policy. Indonesia and Malaysia dominate supply, while India, China and the European Union dominate demand. Policy interventions are common: export taxes and levies, domestic market obligations, biodiesel mandates and sustainability rules all change the return on a tonne of fruit. The companies that do best through a cycle are those with young estates, low cash costs and a balance sheet that lets them keep replanting when prices are low.

The last audited year is the anchor for everything that follows. Revenue was 12,315 IDR bn, cost of revenue was 8,465 IDR bn and gross profit was IDR3,850.0bn [S3, F5, F7]. The cost of revenue includes depreciation and amortisation of 974 IDR bn, which the data pack understated by an order of magnitude, so the first analytical adjustment is to restate the depreciation line to the audited note [S3, F9]. With that correction, EBITDA for the year was IDR3,814.6bn, a margin of 31.0%, and profit attributable to the owners of the parent was 1,840 IDR bn [S3, F13].

**What EBITDA means here, stated once.** Every EBITDA in this report, and every multiple struck on one, is operating EBITDA: audited operating profit plus depreciation of fixed assets and right-of-use assets plus amortisation of bearer plants and intangibles, with the share of the associate's profit excluded, because the valuation already carries that stake at book in the bridge to equity value, and with no add-back of the impairment charge and no deduction of the biological-asset fair-value gain. The model rebuilds that audited base from its own unit costs, margins and D&A charge, and the FY2025A figure of IDR3,814.6bn is the reconstruction, a fraction of a per cent above the audited IDR2,829.4bn plus IDR973.7bn. The audited statements print a higher number: the reconciliation note in the audited accounts shows EBITDA of IDR4,078.0bn, and the whole of the difference reconciles line by line — IDR2,829.4bn of operating profit plus IDR973.7bn of D&A plus the associate's IDR168.4bn plus the IDR116.9bn impairment add-back less the IDR10.4bn biological-asset gain equals IDR4,078.0bn [S3, F52, F64-F67]. We keep our definition rather than adopting the audited reconciliation line for the valuation because the associate's earnings cannot sit inside the multiple while its book value also sits inside the bridge, and because a through-cycle earnings measure should not add back an impairment that the operating accounts carry [S3, F44].

The cost base is the most important number in the model. Cash cost of revenue was the reported cost of revenue less depreciation, and after deducting the cost of the non-palm revenue at a normal margin, the cash cost of a tonne of CPO is about IDR8.0m in the current forecast year; depreciation per tonne is about IDR1.6m, and own capital expenditure per tonne about IDR1.4m [S3, F7, F9, F11]. Each of those is the last-actual unit value from the audited accounts carried forward at the long-run rupiah inflation in the macro deck, not a number observed in the current year; the last actual unit values sit a fortieth lower [S0, S3]. Those three unit numbers drive the forecast; the price and the exchange rate come from the deck [S0, S3].

The cash flow was strong. Operating cash flow was 2,752 IDR bn, own capital expenditure was 856 IDR bn, and the difference funded the dividend of 254 IDR bn and the repayment of debt [S3, F50, F11, F51]. The company also collected more from its plasma programme than it spent on it, which is why the gross capital expenditure line in the pack overstates the true cash cost of investment: the plasma outlay was more than offset by plasma collections in the same investing section [S3, F11]. We therefore use own capital expenditure, not the gross line, in the model [S3, F11].

The nine-month figures show the cycle turning, once they are put on the same operating basis as the annual line. Revenue was 9,110 IDR bn, up slightly, and the printed nine-month EBITDA of 2,950 IDR bn was up by about the same margin [S2, F31, F33]. On our definition the same nine months is operating profit of IDR2,113.5bn plus D&A of IDR733.2bn, and it is up about a per cent year on year; the printed line is higher than it by the associate's IDR144.4bn and a de minimis receivable impairment, and lower by the IDR41.4bn biological-asset gain, which is the identical bridge to the annual note and the reason the printed line must never be compared with an operating forecast without it [S2, F68-F71]. Profit attributable to the owners was 1,442 IDR bn, higher because finance costs fell as debt was repaid [S2, F32]. The margin held at about a third of revenue because the price gain offset the volume loss, which is the operating leverage of an estate working in both directions [S2, S5]. Operating cash flow of 1,912 IDR bn was lower than the prior year because the working-capital release of the previous year reversed, and the company paid the 498 IDR bn dividend [S2, F41, F42].

Our forecast for the current year is deliberately close to the run-rate. We assume CPO sales of 615.0 thousand tonnes, a realised price of US$853.5 a tonne, revenue of IDR12,520.1bn, EBITDA of IDR3,926.0bn and earnings per share of Rp182.2 [S2, S3, S5]. The realised price is the key judgement: the nine-month palm revenue on the nine-month CPO volume implies a rupiah price above the last actual year but well below what the deck's dollar benchmark would suggest once translated at the deck's exchange rate [S2, S4, F31, F34]. That is why our realisation ratio is below the ratio implied by the last audited year, and why the model reproduces the nine-month margin rather than the deck's more optimistic one [S3, S4]. Two of the company-specific inputs therefore sit at the cautious end: the ratio is below the low end of the bracket the nine-month segment revenue implies, and volume is below the company's own projection for the year [S2, F60]. At the low end of that ratio, or at the company's volume projection, the value is a few per cent higher than the base case; we keep the point estimate because at that ratio the year's own volume prices to an operating EBITDA of 3,926.0 within about a per cent of the nine-month operating line scaled to the same volume, and the sensitivity runs are reported in the review record rather than smoothed into the base [S2, F33, F34, F68, F69].

Next year is where the deck does the work. We do not hold the realisation ratio flat: the nine-month accounts show a dollar wedge between the benchmark and the realised price that behaves like a levy-plus-freight amount, so we hold the wedge and let the ratio rise with the benchmark as the deck's price rises [S2, S6]. From beyond the explicit years the convention changes, and we state it rather than leave it implicit: the ratio is held at its final explicit-year level, because the levy and the freight that make up the wedge are themselves reset with the reference price and with dollar costs, so in the terminal years the wedge escalates with the benchmark instead of staying fixed in dollars. The fixed-dollar wedge is therefore a property of the explicit years only, where the November levy schedule is known [S6, F36, F48]. Unit costs escalate with rupiah inflation, and the deck's higher CPO price and exchange rate then flow through, which takes revenue to IDR14,196.9bn and EBITDA to IDR5,276.2bn [S0, S3]. Volume is held flat at the current level because the source the deck rests on says next year is the trough of the Indonesian El Nino effect, and the recovery starts the year after [S8, F37, S5]. That is a large step, and it is the single assumption a reader should challenge; it rests on the GAPKI supply forecast and on the deck's view that the current tightness persists through next year [S8, F37]. If the price instead stays at the current level, the bear case in section five is the relevant valuation [S6].

The balance sheet is in good shape. Net debt at the end of the current year is IDR1,981.5bn on our forecast path, against equity attributable to the owners of 11,481 IDR bn at the last year end, and the debt maturity profile was shortened by the bond repaid during FY2025 [S2, S3, F15]. The company has no material pension deficit, no material lease obligation outside the reported right-of-use assets, and a small non-controlling interest [S2, S3]. The main claims on cash are the dividend, which we assume at a payout of 27.1%, and the replanting budget inside own capital expenditure [S3, F21].

Earnings quality covers three points. First, accruals: profit less operating cash flow over average total assets is negative in both fiscal years and in the nine months, so the company converts more cash than it reports as profit, which is a favourable sign rather than a warning [S3, S2, F13, F14, F32, F50, F41]. Second, cash conversion: operating cash flow has exceeded net profit in every period, although the multiple has fallen from its FY2024 peak as working capital reversed in the nine months [S3, S2, F50, F41]. Third, related-party dealings: purchases from the associate Daiken Dharma Indonesia are 68.0% of raw-material purchases and the payable to it is 30.0% of all trade payables, and no sales to related parties are disclosed [S2, F58, F59]. The IDX status is a standard main-board listing with no special-monitoring board or notation letter disclosed, and the shares sit in the IDX80, Kompas 100 and Jakarta Islamic Index [S4]. The one optics-class item is the land revaluation surplus of 2,585 IDR bn, which inflates book equity but not cash flow [S3, F57].

We value DSNG on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a P/BV cross-check. The DCF carries the controlling weight because the company is a price-taking commodity producer whose value is the present value of a long stream of cash flows at a through-cycle price, and a multiple applied to a single year's EBITDA would capitalise whatever point of the cycle that year happens to sit on [S3, S4]. The EV/EBITDA cross-check carries a smaller weight and the P/BV check the smallest, which is the house weighting for the plantation industry [S3].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck and the house configuration, not from the reporting pack: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, less the Indonesian default spread of 1.6% that the deck deducts from the domestic risk-free rate before it is used as the equity base, plus a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, applied to an unlevered beta of 0.80 that is the house industry default rather than a regression on this stock and relevers to 0.94 at debt of 0.23 times market capitalisation [S2]. That gives a cost of equity of 12.1%. The cost of debt is 9.4% pre-tax, which is the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread of 2.0% [S2]. That loan rate is the marginal rate and is deliberately above the 7.9% average finance cost the income statement carries, which reflects older, cheaper facilities; the marginal rate is the right one for discounting new capital [S3]. At a debt weight of 18.8% the weighted average cost of capital is 11.3% [S2]. We use a terminal growth rate of 2.5%, which is the long-run rupiah inflation in the macro deck and is consistent with a palm price that is flat in real terms after the explicit forecast [S0].

The DCF produces a value of Rp2,991 per share, with the terminal value accounting for 45.7% of enterprise value [S0, S3]. That terminal share is high but not extreme for a long-life estate, and it is the reason we test the terminal assumptions in the sensitivity table rather than treating the output as precise [S3]. The explicit forecast carries free cash flow from IDR2,256.6bn in the current year to IDR2,833.4bn in five years, as the price deck rises and then fades and the cost base escalates with inflation [S0, S3].

The two cross-checks sit below the DCF, and the gap is informative rather than alarming. The EV/EBITDA method applies a multiple of 6.6x to the last actual operating EBITDA of 3,814.6 — the definition section three sets out, not the audited reconciliation line of IDR4,078.0bn — and produces Rp2,267, -24.2% against the primary method [S3, F64]. The P/BV method applies 1.3x to pre-revaluation book equity of IDR9,862.6bn at the balance-sheet date — attributable equity less the land revaluation surplus of IDR2,585.1bn — and produces Rp1,199, -59.9% against the primary method [S2, F62, F63]. Pre-revaluation book is what the house earnings-quality card requires: the surplus (IDR2,585.1bn at the last year end, and unchanged at the balance-sheet date) is an accounting uplift of land values that never reaches cash flow, so applying the peer multiple to the revalued book would flatter this method by roughly a quarter [S3, F57, F62]. Even on the corrected base the method carries the smallest weight and is not a valuation anchor [S3]. The wide gap to the DCF is the point rather than an error: a book multiple on a mature estate cannot see the cash the palms generate between replantings, which is exactly what the discounted cash flow is there to capture, so the cross-check is read as a floor on asset value and not as a competing estimate [S3, S4]. The multiple is a point-in-cycle number, which is why it sits between the two [S3, S4].

One enterprise value, one year, one EBITDA definition: the market multiple quoted in this report is market capitalisation plus our forecast net debt for the current year of IDR1,981.5bn and the minorities, over our FY2026E operating EBITDA of IDR3,926.0bn, which is 4.1x on the forward year [S2, F44]. The numerator and the denominator are on the definition section three sets out, so no reader has to guess which EBITDA the multiple uses; applying the same multiple to the audited reconciliation line of IDR4,078.0bn would give a larger number, which is why the cross-check as struck is the stricter of the two [S3, F64]. On the September spot net debt the same equity capitalises the same earnings at a slightly higher multiple, and deducting the associate stake at book gives a lower one; we quote the forward basis because the target is a forward value, and the cross-check in the table above is struck on the last audited year's operating EBITDA, as it must be [S3, S4, F44].

The sensitivity table shows what matters. A move in the palm price passes more or less straight to the margin, while the same percentage move in volume carries a cost, and a move in the exchange rate has an effect close to a price move because the revenue is dollar-denominated and the cost is rupiah-denominated [S0, S3]. That asymmetry is the reason we treat the exchange rate as a first-order variable in section five rather than as a background assumption [S6, F47]. The grid's centre sits below the published base value because the grid re-runs the DCF with the deck's long-run price held at the shocked level, whereas the base case escalates it with rupiah inflation; read the grid for relative sensitivity, not for the absolute level [S0, S3].

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of the mispricing. At the current price the market is discounting a CPO price of US$1,044/t, below the deck's next-year level, on our cost base and our cost of capital [S0, S3]. In other words, the market is not assuming that the GAPKI supply decline happens; it is assuming that the price stays roughly where it is now and that the cost base does not improve [S8, F37]. If the deck is right, the shares are worth materially more than the price; if the market is right, the shares are worth the bear case, which is below the current price [S3, S6].

The bear case cuts the palm price, trims volumes, strengthens the rupiah and widens the domestic discount, and it values the shares at Rp917, below the current price [S3, S6]. That is the realistic bad outcome rather than a catastrophic one, and it is no longer a mirrored price shock: the exchange-rate and realisation legs were missing from the initiation and are the reason the bear now falls below the price. A deeper trough stress values the equity about a tenth below the bear case, at roughly a third of the base case: it cuts the palm price by a third from the deck's current-year level of US$1,135/t, takes volume and the rupiah a tenth lower each and the realisation a twentieth lower [S6, F47]. That number is floored by the two cross-checks rather than produced by the discounted cash flow: at shocks that deep the explicit free cash flow turns negative and the DCF leg drops out of the blend, so the value is carried by the EV/EBITDA method on the last actual and the P/BV method on pre-revaluation book. The stress therefore understates a true trough rather than representing one, and it is a model floor rather than a claim about the historical low: the reviewed price series in this packet runs back only a few years, so the level is labelled a stress and not a sourced cycle trough [S0, S3]. We run it separately rather than adding a fourth scenario and fold its weight into the bear probability, so the published table stays the three house cases [S3]. The same applies to the policy tail: an export-ban or DMO tightening that closes the domestic outlet is a low-probability event we describe here and do not model as a separate scenario [S6].

The base case values the shares at Rp2,801 and the bull case at Rp4,335, with probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25% respectively [S3]. The bull case carries the two upside legs the report argues: a stronger supply deficit after the GAPKI decline lifts CPO above the deck, El Nino recovery and plasma maturities add volume, the rupiah weakens and the levy-driven domestic discount narrows [S8, S4, S6]. The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers — price, volume, exchange rate and realisation — so the asymmetry in the values comes from the operating leverage of the estate rather than from a different set of assumptions in each case [S3].

The dividend is the market's other anchor. At through-cycle free cash flow the equity generates an FCFE yield of 14.4% against a dividend yield of 3.7%, so the stated payout policy leaves a wide margin of dividend capacity that is not in the price [S3, F21]. The model's net cash build — net debt of -2,484.2 by FY2028 — is reachable as a higher payout or a special dividend rather than stranded, because the capital plan has no large expansion to absorb it [S3, S4]. A payout normalisation is close to neutral for the twelve-month total return in this model, since a larger dividend is offset by a lower ex-dividend value, but it de-risks the return and is the clearest use of the cash [S3].

The first risk is the palm price itself. A sustained fall in the dollar price, whether from a demand shock or from a larger supply response than GAPKI expects, would hit revenue directly and would also widen the domestic discount if the levy is not cut in step [S6, S8]. The second is weather. El Nino has already cut fresh fruit bunch production, and a second dry year would push the volume recovery out by a year and raise the unit cost as fixed costs spread over fewer tonnes [S5, F35]. The third is policy. The export levy, the reference price formula and the biodiesel mandate are all set administratively, and a change in any of them changes the domestic price without changing the company's cost [S6, F36, F48].

The fourth risk is the exchange rate. The rupiah was Rp18,140/USD in early November, close to its weakest on record, and while a weak rupiah helps the revenue line it also raises the rupiah cost of imported fertiliser and fuel [S6, F47]. The fifth is execution: replanting is a multi-year programme that reduces the mature area before it increases it, and a delay in the plasma programme would slow the volume recovery [S4]. The sixth is governance and related-party risk, which we discuss in the next section; the related-party balances are small, but the company is family-controlled and the associate is a related party [S2, S3, F53].

Liquidity is adequate but not deep. The average daily traded value is IDR7.5bn, the free float is 33.1%, and the shares have traded between Rp1,075.0 and Rp1,860.0 over the last year [S0]. A large holder would need patience to build or exit a position, which is a real constraint for an institutional investor even if it is not a valuation input [S0].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A second consecutive quarter of falling fresh fruit bunch production without a price response would push us toward the bear case [S5]. A levy increase that widens the domestic discount would do the same [S6]. A decision to cut the biodiesel mandate, or a failure of the B50 programme to absorb the expected volumes, would remove the domestic demand support that the base case relies on [S6]. On the other side, a confirmed GAPKI output decline and a rising reference price would move us toward the bull case [S8, F48].

DSNG is controlled by two families. The Triputra family interests hold 30.6% and the Oetomo family interests 29.2%, with a further block held by an investment company and the remainder in public hands [S4, S3, F55, F56]. The ultimate beneficiaries named in the annual report are Ny. T.P. Rachmat L.R. Imanto and Andrianto Oetomo, and the president director is a member of the Oetomo family, so the controlling shareholders and the management are the same people [S4]. The public holds 33.1% on the exchange's free-float measure, comfortably above the minimum, and the company is not on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S0, S4].

The audit is clean. The consolidated accounts are audited by Siddharta Widjaja and Rekan, the Indonesian member firm of KPMG, and the opinion is unmodified in all material respects [S4, S3]. The board includes independent commissioners alongside the executive directors, and the annual report discloses the directors' shareholdings, which are concentrated in the two families [S4]. There is no dual-class share structure and no material pledge of shares disclosed [S4].

Related-party dealings are modest at the balance-sheet level. Trade payables to related parties were 2.0 IDR bn at the end of September, against third-party payables many times larger, and the associated estate is a related party because the company holds a stake in it [S2, S3, F53, F44]. The company lent to that associate in the past, but the loan was repaid in full in April 2025, so the related-party receivable is no longer a financing exposure [S3]. The share of the associate's profit is disclosed separately and is not buried in operating income [S3, F52].

The dividend record is consistent. The company declared Rp47.0/share for the last financial year and Rp24.0/share for the year before, a payout of about 27.1% of earnings, and it paid both in the July after the annual meeting [S3, F21, F22]. The dividend is covered by free cash flow in our forecast, and the payout is inside the stated policy band [S3, F50, F11]. A family-controlled company that pays a consistent cash dividend is less likely to divert cash into related-party projects, which is the main governance risk in this structure [S3].

On ESG, the certification stack is the strongest part of the story. Every mill is ISPO certified, most are RSPO certified, and the nucleus estates are certified at a high share under both schemes [S4]. The company was the first palm oil producer to receive impact investment financing from the &Green fund, and it operates a bio-compressed natural gas plant that captures mill effluent, which is a genuine emissions reduction rather than a disclosure exercise [S4]. The plasma programme is the social licence component: it gives smallholders a stake in the estate and reduces the risk of land conflict [S4, F38].

The ESG exposures that remain are the ones common to the industry. Deforestation rules in Europe affect the export market for palm products, although the company's certification coverage mitigates the risk [S4]. The wood-products business sells into Europe and North America, where demand for engineered flooring has been weak, which is a commercial rather than an ESG risk [S7]. Labour intensity is high, with 19,037 employees, and the estate is in regions where labour and land disputes are common, so the plasma and certification programmes are also risk management [S0, S4].

The nearest catalyst is the monthly policy reset. The Ministry of Trade sets the reference price, the export duty and the levy each month, and the November package cut the charge to US$246/t while the reference price fell to US$979/t; the two moved together, so net export parity was flat and the change was neutral for the domestic price rather than positive [S6, F36, F48]. What matters for the fourth quarter is the December reference price and whether the levy falls with it: a higher reference price, or a levy cut that is not offset, would support the realised price and validate the base case [S6, F48].

The second catalyst is the fourth-quarter production report. The nine-month fresh fruit bunch decline was driven by El Nino in Kalimantan, and the fourth quarter is seasonally the strongest, so the report will show whether the volume recovery has started [S5, F35]. A stabilisation in fresh fruit bunch production, combined with a firm price, would be the combination that closes the gap between the market's implied price and the deck [S8].

The third catalyst is the full-year result and the dividend. The company reports in the first quarter and proposes a dividend at the annual meeting in the middle of the year, and on our forecast the dividend per share rises to Rp49 over the next twelve months, a yield of 3.7% at the current price [S3, F21]. A dividend increase in line with earnings would be a tangible signal that the board shares our view of the cycle [S3].

The fourth catalyst is the GAPKI data flow. The association publishes production, export and stock data monthly, and the 2027 output forecast of a 2,200 kt decline will be tested against the actual harvest as the year progresses [S8, F37]. A confirmed decline would support the deck's price path; a smaller decline would push us toward the bear case [S8].

Between updates we monitor five things: the monthly reference price and levy, the company's quarterly fresh fruit bunch and CPO volumes, the realised price per tonne implied by the segment revenue, the unit cash cost per tonne, and the net debt path [S6, S5, S2, S3]. The first two are the cycle, the middle two are the company's execution, and the last is the balance-sheet constraint. If the realised price and the unit cost both move in the company's favour, the earnings upgrade is mechanical; if they diverge, the cost line is the one to watch [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: CPO sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 615 kt: nine-month CPO production of 451 kt [F34] annualises to about 601 kt and Q4 is seasonally the strongest quarter, so 615 kt sits between that run-rate and the company's own FY2026 projection of +1% on the FY2025 realisation, about 637 kt [F60, S4 p.129]. The 651 kt printed in the same table is the FY2025 TARGET, which the 631 kt realisation missed [F46, F23]; it is not a current-year work plan, and the earlier reading of it as one is corrected here. FY2027E is held flat at 615 kt because GAPKI says the 2.2m-tonne Indonesian decline in 2027 is the full El Nino effect [F37, S8] and DSNG's own nine-month FFB is down 4.3% with Q3 down 5.7% q/q [F35, S5]; the recovery starts in FY2028E as the affected blocks and the 29,000 ha of plasma estates mature, reaching 645 kt by FY2030E against planted area of 111,900 ha [F38].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 palm-segment revenue of 8,059.213 [S2] on 451 kt of CPO production [F34] is Rp17.87m per tonne; CPO sales track production (FY2025 sales 628.737 kt against production 631.046 kt, 99.6% [F1, F23]), so the production denominator is immaterial. Stripping by-products at the FY2025 per-tonne value (1,748.322 of non-CPO palm revenue on 628.737 kt = Rp2.781m [F5, F29]) leaves Rp15.09m per tonne of CPO, or USD 859/t at the deck's FY2026E rupiah of 17,570 and USD 917/t at the FY2025 actual 16,448 [F3]. That brackets the ratio at 0.757-0.808 of the USD 1,135/t benchmark; we use 0.752 for FY2026E because at that ratio the model's FY2026E operating EBITDA of 3,926.0 lands within about a per cent of the nine-month operating line — the printed note-41 2,949.803 [F33] less the associate's 144.430 [F70] plus the biological-asset gain 41.395 [F71] — scaled to the year's volume, and the 0.808 upper bound is the sensitivity. From FY2027E we hold the dollar wedge fixed at the nine-month 281.5 USD/t rather than the ratio: the November reference price of 978.90 less the 246.36 levy gives net export parity of 732.5 against 733.9 in October [F48, F36], so the wedge is a levy-plus-freight amount, not a proportional haircut, and the ratio rises as the benchmark rises. Beyond the explicit years the ratio is held at its final explicit-year level (lt 0.761) rather than the wedge, because the levy and the freight are themselves reset with the reference price and with dollar costs, so the wedge escalates with the benchmark in the terminal years; the fixed-dollar wedge is a property of the explicit years only, where the November levy schedule is known.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No domestic price cap applies to CPO; the DMO obligation is on producers' export allocation, not on the price received.

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (bcm per tonne equivalent)
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 so that cost_per_bcm is read directly as rupiah of cash cost per tonne of CPO sold; DSNG is an estate, not a mine, and there is no overburden to strip.

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cash COGS = cost of revenue 8,464.728 less D&A 973.744 = 7,490.984 [F7, F9]; less the cost of the 3,216.888 of non-CPO revenue at a 20% gross margin = 2,573.510, leaving 4,917.474 for 628.737 kt = Rp7.821m per tonne [F1, F29]. Escalated at the 2.5% long-run rupiah inflation in the macro deck.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of cash cost
assumptions.basis: No separate fuel index is modelled: diesel is inside the rupiah cash cost per tonne, which already carries the FY2025 actual fuel bill.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: haulage, milling and overhead are already inside the audited cost of revenue from which cost_per_bcm is derived, so adding a second per-tonne charge would double-count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: No royalty: Indonesian oil-palm estates pay the export levy only on exports, and the geographic segment note shows the entire palm-oil line, 8,059.213 in the nine months, sold into the local market with nil export sales [F61, S2]. The levy therefore reaches DSNG through the domestic price, not as a charge on its own sales [F36].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (PK, PKO, wood products, renewables)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-CPO revenue 3,216.888 = consolidated revenue 12,314.712 less CPO revenue 9,097.824 [F5, F29]; escalated at 2.5% rupiah inflation, with no volume growth assumed for the wood and renewable segments.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: 20% is the blend across the whole non-CPO line, not the wood-and-renewables margin. FY2025: palm segment revenue 10,846.146 and gross profit 3,660.509, wood 1,242.325 and 138.887 (11.2%), renewables 226.241 and 50.588 (22.4%) [S3]. The non-CPO line is PK/PKO 1,748.322 plus wood and renewables 1,468.566; at the palm-segment margin on PK/PKO and the reported margins on the other two, the blend is 20.0% and reconciles the group gross profit of 3,849.984 [S3]. Nine-month 2026: palm 8,059.213 and 2,826.156 (35.1%), wood 897.400 and 49.676 (5.5%), renewables 153.196 and 35.212 (23.0%) [S2]; the wood margin halved but the palm margin rose, so the same blend still holds. The red team's 8.1% is the wood-plus-renewables subset only, 1,050.596 of 9,109.809 revenue.

assumptions.label: D&A per tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A 973.744 [F9] over 628.737 kt of CPO sold [F1] = Rp1.549m per tonne; escalated at 2.5% rupiah inflation. The pack's Rp65.922bn D&A line is not a D&A figure and is restated to the audited note.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 own capex 856.267 = fixed-asset additions 648.177 + capitalised plantation cost 208.090 [F11] over 628.737 kt [F1] = Rp1.362m per tonne. The plasma outlay of 943.660 is excluded because the 1,019.857 of plasma collections in the same investing section reimburses it [F11]. Escalated at 2.5%.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no separately disclosed expansion project is funded in the plan; the company's 2026 budget is maintenance and replanting, which sits in capex_unit.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital 1,144.975 / revenue 12,314.712 = 9.3%; the three-year average of 11.5% is inflated by the FY2022 inventory build, so the last actual is used.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax 670.747 / pre-tax profit 2,499.545 = 26.8%, held flat; the group has no material deferred-tax asset to run down.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance costs 452.485 [F18] / opening debt 5,733.094 = 7.9%; the 2020 sustainability bond of 181.924 was repaid during FY2025 (bonds payable nil at 31-Dec-2025, 181.924 at 31-Dec-2024, and 181.924 repaid in the FY2025 cash flow) [S3], and the remaining bank debt reprices off JIBOR, so the rate is held.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income 12.552 [F19] / opening cash 557.023 = 2.25%; most operating cash sits in current accounts rather than time deposits.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: debt fell from 5,733.094 to 4,105.200 in FY2025 and to 3,247.177 by 30-Sep-2026 [S2], and the stated policy is deleveraging, so no new net debt is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating line; the FY2025 gap between reported pre-tax profit and EBIT less net interest is the capitalised-interest adjustment, which is not a run-rate item.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: the non-controlling interest is Rp139.699bn of equity and its share of profit was negative in FY2025, so it is immaterial to the parent valuation.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp47 [F21] on EPS of Rp173.63 (profit 1,840.490 [F13] over 10,599.8424m shares [F20]) = 27.1%, inside the stated 25-30% policy band.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 10,599,842,400 shares issued and outstanding with no buyback or option overhang disclosed [F20].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%: the long-run rupiah inflation in the macro deck, consistent with a terminal CPO price that is flat in real terms and a mature estate that cannot outgrow the planting base.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 SG&A and other opex 1,009.092 / revenue 12,314.712 = 8.19%; the three-year average of 8.96% is lifted by the FY2022-23 cost base, so the last actual is used.

challenges.challenge: The realisation of 0.752 carries the valuation and is the floor of the peer set (qualified peers median about 0.865; own FY2025 0.874), yet its derivation divides nine-month palm-segment revenue of 8,059.213 by nine-month CPO *production* of 451 kt and translates at the FY2026E deck rate of 17,570 rather than the nine-month average JISDOR; the published ASP is per tonne sold (628.7 kt sales against 631.0 kt production in FY2025). Holding the ratio flat also forces the dollar wedge to widen from 133 USD/t (FY2025) and 282 (9M2026) to 308 at the FY2027E benchmark, with no evidence that the discount is proportional rather than a fixed levy-plus-freight amount.
challenges.answer: The ratio finding stands and the bracket is unchanged, but the calibration wording is corrected for the EBITDA definition: 0.752 is set so that the model's FY2026E operating EBITDA of 3,926.0 lands within about a per cent of the nine-month operating line — the printed note-41 2,949.8 less the associate's 144.4 plus the biological-asset gain 41.4 — scaled to the year's volume, not to the printed 2,949.8 itself [F33, F68, F69, F70, F71]. The 0.80 and 0.85 targets quoted earlier were struck on the pre-rebuild model; the rebuilt calibrated base is Rp2,800.6 and the ratio uplift remains a few per cent of value, not a rating changer [S2, S3].

challenges.challenge: The bear shocks CPO x0.8 and volume x0.95 but holds the exchange rate at the deck, although section 4 calls the exchange rate a first-order variable. The model's own grid gives Rp1,088 at CPO x0.8 with IDR x0.9, 18% below the Rp1,325 price, so the sentence 'the bear case still values the shares at Rp1,490, above the current price, which is why we are comfortable with the rating' depends on assuming the rupiah stays at its weakest on record.
challenges.answer: Added m.usd_idr x0.9 to the bear and x1.1 to the bull, plus a.realisation x0.95/x1.05, mirrored. On the rebuilt model the bear values the shares at Rp916.8, below the Rp1,325 price, and the 'bear above the price' sentences are removed from the summary, thesis, section 4 and section 5. Probabilities stay 25/50/25; the weighted target is Rp2,713 [S6, F47, S3].

challenges.challenge: The bear is a mirrored 20% price shock, not a stress test of the commodity's downside. Nothing establishes that a 20% fall is the worst realistic case for a price-taking estate, and no scenario tests a trough CPO around USD700-800 or an export ban/DMO tightening, even though DSNG sells 100% of its palm output domestically (S2/S3 geographic note) and 88% of revenue is palm.
challenges.answer: Ran a trough stress separately: CPO x0.65, volume x0.9, FX x0.9, realisation x0.95 gives Rp837.2 on the rebuilt model, below the mirrored bear of Rp916.8; the policy tail (export ban or DMO tightening) is described in section 5 and its weight folded into the bear's 25% because the engine has no export-ban driver. Section 5 also now states that the stress is floored by the EV/EBITDA and P/BV legs because the DCF drops out at those shocks [S6, S8, F36, F48].

challenges.challenge: FY2027E volume rises 2.4% (630 versus 615 kt) as 'El Nino-affected blocks recover', but the source the price deck rests on (S8) says the 2.2m t Indonesian decline in 2027 is the *full* El Nino effect, and the company's own nine-month FFB is down 4.3% with Q3 down 5.7% q/q (S5). The model therefore has DSNG's volume recovering into the year the source says is the trough, at unchanged unit cost. Separately, FY2026E volume of 615 kt is below the company's own 2026 projection (AR table: +1% on 631 kt, about 637 kt); 651 kt is the 2025 target, which was missed.
challenges.answer: FY2027E volume held flat at 615 kt; recovery starts FY2028E (625/635/645 kt) as the affected blocks and 29,000 ha of plasma mature. F46 is the 2026 work plan of 651 kt, 3.2% above the FY2025 actual of 631.046 kt, not a 2025 target; the nine-month 451 kt makes it optimistic. GAPKI's 2.2m t 2027 decline is the full El Nino effect and DSNG's own FFB is down 4.3% with Q3 down 5.7% q/q.

challenges.challenge: The report calls the November levy cut 'a meaningful positive for the domestic price' and a catalyst. The same article sets the reference price 6.07% lower at USD978.90; net export parity is 978.90 - 246.36 = 732.5 USD/t against roughly 1,042 - 308.27 = 733.9 in October, essentially unchanged, and the article's own point is that exporters keep more while the rupiah benefit depends on B50. The one-sided read flatters the policy backdrop.
challenges.answer: Rewrote section 2 and section 7: the November levy cut to 246.36 was offset by the reference price falling to 978.90, so net export parity was 732.5 vs 733.9 in October, essentially flat. The levy cut is neutral for the domestic price, not a positive; the December reset matters only if the reference price rises or the levy falls without an offset.

challenges.challenge: The P/BV cross-check applies 1.289x to book equity of Rp12,447.6bn that includes the Rp2,585.1bn revaluation surplus (S3 note 16, revaluation model for land adopted December 2020). The house card is explicit that P/BV work uses pre-revaluation book. On pre-revaluation equity of about Rp9,863bn the method produces about Rp1,084, not Rp1,514, and the published target falls by roughly Rp70.
challenges.answer: The 1.289x is the average of the peer median and DSNG's own five-year average of reported P/BV; the plantation peers carry PSAK 16 land revaluations too, so the multiple and the book must be on the same basis or the comparison is inconsistent. We disclose the 2,585.051 surplus (F57) and state in section 4 that the P/BV line is an upper bound; on pre-revaluation book at the same multiple the method is worth about Rp1,199 (FY2025 book 9,863 x 1.289 / 10.600bn shares), not the Rp1,084 quoted, which uses 30-Sep equity that still carries a 2,754.595 surplus. The method has a 0.15 weight and is not a target anchor, so the target does not rest on it.

challenges.challenge: The model shows net cash of Rp2,305bn by FY2028 and Rp18tn by FY2035 while paying out only 27.1%, and the company doubled DPS from 24 to 47 in FY2025 on a stated 25-30% policy. Neither the base nor the bull case tests a payout normalisation, special dividend or buyback, and the commodity-cyclical output contract's dividend-capacity yield against the NAV anchor is missing, so the return-of-capital upside is invisible.
challenges.answer: Added the dividend-capacity statement: FCFE yield 14.4% against a dividend yield of 3.7%, so the 27.1% payout leaves wide capacity; the net cash build to FY2028 is reachable as a higher payout or special dividend because the capital plan has no large expansion. A 50% payout run gives a target of Rp2,720 vs Rp2,766, with the total return roughly unchanged because the higher DPS offsets the lower ex-div value; it de-risks rather than adds to the twelve-month return. The bull narrative now names payout normalisation.

challenges.challenge: The bull shocks only CPO x1.2 and volume x1.05. It does not include the two upside legs the report itself argues: a narrower domestic discount as the export levy falls (the realisation ratio is held at 0.752 in every year and every scenario), and a weaker rupiah. The report's own sensitivity shows FX x1.1 alone adds about Rp930 to the value, larger than the entire bull premium, so the bull understates the case it is meant to test.
challenges.answer: Added the two missing legs to the bull: m.usd_idr x1.1 and a.realisation x1.05, mirrored in the bear at x0.9 and x0.95. On the rebuilt model the bull values the shares at Rp4,335.0 against Rp3,522 before the rebuild; the FX leg alone is worth about Rp930 on the grid, as noted [S6, F47, S3].

challenges.challenge: Three checkable statements are wrong. (i) The FY2025 bond is said to have been repaid in January 2026, but S3 shows bonds payable at zero at 31-Dec-2025 and Rp181.924bn repaid in the FY2025 cash flow. (ii) Section 1 says the palm segment was 88% of 'consolidated revenue of 12,315 IDR bn in the first nine months'; nine-month revenue is 9,109.809 (F31). (iii) The thesis says nine-month EBITDA of 2,950 is within a rounding error of the full-year base case of 3,926, when it is within rounding of the annualised 3,933.
challenges.answer: Corrected all three. (i) The 2020 bond of 181.924 was repaid during FY2025 (bonds payable nil at 31-Dec-2025, 181.924 at 31-Dec-2024, 181.924 repaid in the FY2025 cash flow), not January 2026; fixed in section 1, section 3, post_bs_review and the cost_of_debt basis. (ii) Nine-month revenue is 9,109.809 (F31), not 12,314.712; section 1 now cites F31. (iii) The thesis now says the nine-month EBITDA annualises to the full-year base case, not that it is within rounding of it.

challenges.challenge: Other_margin is held at 20%, citing FY2025 wood 11.2% and renewables 22.4%, but the nine-month segment note shows wood at 5.5% (49.676 on 897.400) and renewables at 23.0% (35.212 on 153.196), a blended 8.1% on the non-palm segments. The cited wood margin has halved and the 20% blend is not reconciled to the latest actual.
challenges.answer: The 8.1% is the wood-plus-renewables subset only (1,050.596 of 9,109.809 revenue). The 20% applies to the whole non-CPO line, which also carries PK/PKO of 1,748.322 at the palm-segment margin. FY2025: palm 10,846.146/3,660.509 (33.8%), wood 1,242.325/138.887 (11.2%), renewables 226.241/50.588 (22.4%); 9M2026: palm 8,059.213/2,826.156 (35.1%), wood 897.400/49.676 (5.5%), renewables 153.196/35.212 (23.0%). The blend is 20.0% in FY2025 and 22.8% in 9M2026, so 20% is sourced and conservative; the wood margin halved but the palm margin rose. The basis and section 3 now show the separation.

challenges.challenge: Three different EV/EBITDA figures appear: 'a little over 4.1x' in the summary, 4.3x in the extreme-call justification (EV Rp16.7tn, market cap plus net debt, without minorities or the associate), and 3.89x implied by the bridge's own EV of Rp15.27tn after the Rp1,579bn associate and Rp140bn minorities.
